newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Relief crew heads for Mir, old team makes repairs.
newsitem.headline: Relief crew heads for Mir, old team makes repairs.

text.p: Two Russian relief cosmonauts were orbiting the Earth on Wednesday, gradually aligning themselves with the ailing Mir space station where they plan to make repairs that will determine the craft's future.
"Everything is proceeding normally," Mission Control spokesman Valery Lyndin said on Wednesday morning. "The new crew are already on their 11th orbit around Earth."
Commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov are due to link up with Mir at 1703 GMT on Thursday after their Tuesday launch.

As they sped towards Mir, an adviser to President Boris Yeltsin said Russia should continue to fund Mir. The adviser, Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, said the station was a useful training ground for an international space station which is being built.
The current crew on Wednesday continued repairs on the Elektron oxygen generating system that has not worked since last week, NASA spokeswoman Kathleen Maliga said.
On board Mir the crew of two Russians and one American were using solid fuel oxygen generators called 'candles' as they were unable to restart the newer Elektron on board.
It failed to work last week and they have still not resolved the problem, which NASA believes is caused by a faulty pressure regulator, officials said.

Mir's older back-up oxygen generator is not available for use because it is located in the Kvant-2 module, which the crew powered down to save energy after the space station collided with its supply ship on June 25, causing a major loss of power.

The Mir crew of commander Vasily Tsibliyev, engineer Alexander Lazutkin and British-born U.S. physicist Michael Foale were planning on Wednesday to undock their Progress cargo ship to make room for the new crew.
"The Mir crew is making preparations to meet the new crew and to depart. These are their two main tasks today," Lyndin said.
The new crew will relink to Progress after Tsibliyev and Lazutkin return to Earth on August 14 after 185 days in space.
Solovyov, 49, one of Russia's most experienced cosmonauts with a total of 456 days in space, and space newcomer Vinogradov, 43, will undertake vital repairs on the Mir soon after their arrival.

On August 20, the two men, with Vinogradov leading the way, will open the hatch to the dark, airless Spektr module which was damaged in the June 25 accident and attempt to reconnect cables that link up to Spektr's solar panels.
If Solovyov and Vinogradov succeed in the task, then they can power up the Kvant-2 again and use its oxygen system and other equipment.

The job is risky. Space officials say the module, which is now sealed off from the rest of Mir, could contain dangerous floating chemicals or debris. A puncture in a space suit could mean a swift death.

Shaposhnikov, who advises Yeltsin on space and aviation, told a news conference Russia should continue to operate and fund Mir as a training ground for the Alpha international space station which is due to be assembled in stages by 2003.

Mir "is the base of the international space station which is called Alpha," he said. "The station has considerable work experience, but nonetheless survives under these conditions, and overcomes all of these influences that arise."

"If it was stopped because of some holding back of pennies, let's say, we could lose millions and a very interesting international programme, since not a single country in the world has the experience we have," he said.
